gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured accuracy figure from a named tester. 3D Printing Industry measured the 3DMakerpro Seal on a 15 × 20 × 25 mm reference block in turntable mode and got 0.02 mm on X and Z but -0.16 mm on Y, 16 times its 0.01 mm claim. CNC Kitchen measured the Creality CR-Scan Raptor on a 100.25 mm ball bar and got 100.22 to 100.25 mm, at most 0.03 mm off.
standout_why: I opened three of the four cited pages: 3dprinting.com/scanners/best-small-format-3d-scanners, makermachinesatlas.com best-3d-scanner-for-small-objects-and-jewelry and comparefoundry.com light-source-accuracy-claims-and-us-packages. All three give only maker specs. Each says so itself ('All numbers are manufacturer specs', 'not our measurements', 'not independently tested'). The fourth cited page, print3dindex.com, returned 403. The top result I opened, 3dprinterworld.com's MINI 2 review, has no measurements of its own either. None of these pages gives a measured deviation for any candidate. ChatGPT's own answer also says its figures are 'manufacturer specifications, not guaranteed real-world results'.
decides: This makes the page more trustworthy without changing the ranking. It qualifies the Seal's '0.01 mm' headline: in a named test it held 0.02 mm on two axes but missed by 0.16 mm on the third, on a 25 mm block. That still suits figures and 3D printing but not tight-tolerance small parts. It also gives the Raptor the only artifact-verified result among the candidates (0.03 mm over 100 mm), which supports it as the pick for mechanical parts. The only reviewer figure for the MINI 2 is a general 'within 0.05 mm of CAD' with no per-object numbers. Its 'best for tiny detail' placing therefore rests on maker specs, and the page should say so. Store prices checked today also undercut what ChatGPT showed: Seal $454 and Seal Lite $215, against $559.99 or about $450–700 for the Seal in ChatGPT's answer.

findings.label: Measured deviation on a reference cuboid, turntable mode (3D Printing Industry, Alex Tyrer-Jones)
findings.value: 0.02 mm on X and Z; -0.16 mm on Y
findings.source_title: Review: 3DMakerpro Seal, an affordable, user-friendly and high quality 3D scanner (3D Printing Industry)
findings.note: Review dated 2024-02-08. The block's known size was 15 × 20 × 25 mm and the scan was compared against it. The maker claims 0.01 mm, so the Y-axis error is 16 times the claim.

findings.label: Measured deviation on real parts (3D Printing Industry, Alex Tyrer-Jones)
findings.value: -0.053 mm (motorcycle indicator); 0.104 mm (leg height of an e-scooter suspension part)
findings.source_title: Review: 3DMakerpro Seal, an affordable, user-friendly and high quality 3D scanner (3D Printing Industry)
findings.note: Review dated 2024-02-08. The review does not state the parts' nominal sizes or the scan mode for these two parts.

findings.label: Ball-bar length accuracy (CNC Kitchen, Stefan Hermann)
findings.value: 100.24, 100.25 and 100.22 mm against a 100.25 mm nominal; at most 0.03 mm per 100 mm
findings.source_title: 10 Tips for Better 3D Scans (feat. Creality CR-Scan Raptor), CNC Kitchen
findings.note: Post dated 2024-09-14. The DIY ball bar was two 10 mm bearings on a carbon rod, with the nominal derived from calipers, scanned in three orientations. The page says this is about 0.3 mm per metre. The scan mode for this test is not stated in the text I read. The test object is 100 mm, not a small part.

findings.label: Resolution used for a coin scan (CNC Kitchen)
findings.value: 0.02 mm (highest laser-mode setting) on a 50-cent euro coin; default laser mode is 0.15 mm
findings.source_title: 10 Tips for Better 3D Scans (feat. Creality CR-Scan Raptor), CNC Kitchen
findings.note: Post dated 2024-09-14. The page also says laser mode needs at least 4 markers in frame at all times and has a scan field of about 20 cm diagonal.
